summary: Mobile IPv4 uses a home agent to anchor a roaming device's sessions. This document adds messaging so a home agent can be assigned dynamically, or a device can be redirected to a better one, while leaving the selection method open. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: When you travel, the post office forwards your mail through one helper. This lets the system pick a helper close to you, or switch you to a better one, as you move.

subtitle: How a roaming Mobile IPv4 device asks the network to pick its home agent, or gets redirected to a better one.

tldr.problem: In Mobile IPv4 a roaming device is tied to a home agent, which may be far away and is cumbersome to configure and balance across a large deployment.
tldr.mechanism: The device sets the Home Agent field to a special all-zero or all-ones address, optionally adds a Requested HA Extension, and the home agent either accepts or rejects with a redirect code carrying a Redirected HA Extension.
tldr.outcome: The network can assign an optimal home agent for a session, while how it chooses one is left open.

today: RFC 4433 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on Mobile IPv4 as defined in RFC 3344.

sections.title: The Problem with a Fixed Home Agent
sections.content:
Mobile IPv4 (RFC 3344) uses a home agent (HA) to anchor the sessions of a roaming mobile node (MN). RFC 4433 adds a messaging mechanism for dynamic HA assignment and HA redirection during initial registration, with the goal of assigning an optimal HA to a session.

The RFC lists reasons this matters. A distant HA means long signaling delay and tunneled traffic that travels far. Provisioning many HA addresses on mobile nodes is cumbersome in a large deployment. The network may also want load balancing among several HAs, and local administrative policy may apply.

The old discovery method, a subnet-directed broadcast in the Home Agent field, is unlikely to reach the home subnet because routers drop such packets by default.
sections.plainLanguage: If your helper lives far away, everything takes a long trip. It is better to get a helper nearby, without carrying a long list of helpers.

sections.title: Scope and Terms
sections.content:
The RFC defines the messaging, not how the network picks an HA. Selection can be done by any node that sees the Registration Request, such as a foreign agent, AAA server or home agent, using criteria like load balancing, geographic proximity or policy. Distributing a security association between the MN and HA is also out of scope.

Three roles are named. The Requested HA is the unicast address the Registration Request is sent to. The Assigned HA is the HA that accepts the request and returns a successful reply. The Redirected HA is the HA named in a redirect rejection.

The special value ALL-ZERO-ONE-ADDR means 0.0.0.0 or 255.255.255.255. The latter indicates a preference for an HA in the home domain, and the former indicates no preference between home and visited domain. The MN MUST use the NAI extension when requesting a dynamically assigned HA.
sections.plainLanguage: Three helper roles: the one you ask first, the one who actually takes the job, and the one you are sent to if the first says to go elsewhere.

sections.title: The Dynamic HA Extension
sections.content:
The Dynamic HA Extension carries the address of an HA and can appear in Registration Requests and Replies. It is a skippable extension with type DYNAMIC-HA-ADDRESS (139), a subtype, a length (always 4 bytes) and the HA-Address.

Subtype 1 is the Requested HA Extension, which the MN may add as a hint about where it wants to be anchored. It MUST hold a valid unicast address. Subtype 2 is the Redirected HA Extension, which says where the MN should attempt its next registration. It MUST be present in a Registration Reply whose code is REDIRECT-HA-REQ.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a small note stuck onto a request. One kind says which helper you would like. The other says which helper to go to instead.

sections.title: Assignment and Redirection
sections.content:
For dynamic assignment, the MN sets the Home Agent field to ALL-ZERO-ONE-ADDR and sends the request, directly or via the foreign agent (FA), to the Requested HA. The HA processes it under Mobile IPv4 and, if successful, creates a binding and puts its own address in the reply. That address is the Assigned HA, which the MN uses for the rest of the session, including renewals.

For redirection, the HA may reject a request with the field set to ALL-ZERO-ONE-ADDR, even if it authenticates, using code REDIRECT-HA-REQ and a Redirected HA Extension. The MN authenticates the reply, then registers with the Redirected HA, which it MUST list in the Requested HA Extension. If a loop occurs, with the Redirected HA being one that already redirected the MN, the MN stops and indicates that a loop was detected. How many Redirected HAs it remembers is an implementation parameter.

If the MN knows an HA address, it can place it in the Requested HA Extension as a hint.
sections.plainLanguage: You ask a helper. They either say yes and become your helper, or point you to another helper. If you keep going in circles, you stop and report it.

sections.title: Mobile Node, Foreign Agent and Home Agent Behavior
sections.content:
The mobile node MUST use the NAI extension (so its Home Address field is 0.0.0.0) and MUST protect the request with a valid authenticator. Using a short lifetime, for example 5 seconds, helps limit multiple bindings. With a co-located care-of address, the Requested HA Extension MUST contain the HA the request is sent to. After a session ends, the MN may clear the cached Assigned HA to get a new, possibly better HA next time.

The foreign agent MUST forward the request to the address in the Requested HA Extension. If it cannot find a Requested HA, or the address is not a routable unicast address, it rejects with NONZERO-HA-REQD.

The home agent creates one mobility binding per MN. If the Requested HA Extension does not match the request's destination, it MUST reject with error code 136. A request to a unicast destination with ALL-ZERO-ONE-ADDR in the HA field is not rejected with code 136, which avoids the multiple-responder problem of subnet-directed broadcast.
sections.plainLanguage: Each player has a job: the traveler writes the request, the local agent passes it along, and the home helper says yes or points elsewhere.

sections.title: Picking the Requested HA and Legacy Nodes
sections.content:
The RFC gives examples of how the Requested HA might be learned: from DHCP Mobile IP Home Agent Option 68, from a AAA server via the FA, from a DNS lookup of an HA hostname, or from static configuration followed by a possible redirect.

A legacy HA may reject the request with code 136. A legacy FA may forward the request with the destination set to ALL-ZERO-ONE-ADDR, so it may be dropped. If the MN gets no reply, or error code 70 (poorly formed request), it should fall back to sending the request with the Home Agent field set to a known HA address and the same address in the Requested HA Extension. A legacy MN that does not use ALL-ZERO-ONE-ADDR stays on its statically configured HA as in RFC 3344.
sections.plainLanguage: If an old post office does not understand the new form, you fall back to writing the helper's address on the envelope the old way.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC does not change the Mobile IPv4 security model. It assumes a security configuration already exists between the MN and HA, or is created with the first request as described in RFC 3957. Requests and replies are protected by authenticators, and the Assigned HA authenticates each request just as in Mobile IPv4.

One new risk is described: a man in the middle could capture a request with the HA field set to ALL-ZERO-ONE-ADDR and forward it to other HAs, so more than one HA creates a binding. The rogue node would need to know suitable HA addresses and replay within the replay window. It is only possible when the Requested HA Extension is absent, and a short request lifetime, for example 5 seconds, reduces the exposure.
sections.plainLanguage: A sneaky person could copy your request and send it to many helpers. Writing a short expiry on it and naming your helper makes that much harder.
